newsitem.title: MEXICO: Labor leader's death stirs emotions in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Labor leader's death stirs emotions in Mexico.

text.p: The death of Fidel Velazquez, Mexico's most powerful labour boss, has elicited mixed emotions from the country's political factions and prompted speculation it may hurt the ruling PRI.

As mourners ranging from veteran labour leaders in chauffeur-driven limousines to workers in factory overalls filed past his coffin late on Saturday, some of his detractors were already trying to make political gain.

"Don Fidel", as Velazquez was known by friends and enemies alike, was a controversial figure who wielded enormous power in national politics and for more than half a century kept Mexico's union movement firmly in the pocket of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

He died on Saturday of heart and respiratory failure at the age of 97, still heading the six-million-strong Mexican Workers Confederation (CTM) that has been a pillar of support for the PRI for most of its 68 years in power.

Members of the PRI elite who paid final respects to Velazquez praised a man who built up the labour movement, helped create social security, promoted the vote for women and also kept workers in line in the interests of national stability.

But his death robbed them of a key ally just two weeks before mid-term Congressional elections on July 6, when the PRI could lose its decades-old majority in the lower house. Opposition politicians were quick to seize on the loss.

"First, (I hope) he goes to heaven, and second, that he takes to the grave the old Mexican political system," Vicente Fox, an opposition state governor of the conservative National Action Party, told reporters.
"We cannot rejoice over the disappearance of a human being, but we believe a symbol has died," the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution added in a cutting statement.
"Fidel Velazquez embodied a labour practice ... characterised by its alliance with power, always obedient to one government after the next, anti-democratic and intolerant," it said.

Radio reports noted that the workers who came to CTM headquarters to file past his coffin -- some patently upset -- did not represent a mass turnout, and only a few of the 11,000 unions grouped under the confederation's umbrella showed up.
On Sunday, President Ernesto Zedillo was due to pay his last respects before the former milkman is buried in the humble village outside Mexico City where he was born in 1900.

"Don Fidel dedicated his life to organising workers in demand and defence of their rights," Zedillo said in an affectionate statement. "He knew how to reconcile the special interests of workers with the general interests of the nation."

Immediately after Velazquez's death on Saturday morning, the CTM moved quickly to quash any hint of a power struggle. It named deputy secretary-general Leonardo Rodriguez Alcaine as successor, at least until a ballot is held next February.
But PRI leaders who visited the coffin were inevitably forced to deny suggestions from reporters that Velazquez's death would deal a blow to the party in the July 6 vote.

Earlier this year, the cigar-chomping labour veteran had ordered the CTM's members to vote for the PRI, describing any backing for the opposition as an act of "treason" that would be met with explusion from its ranks.
He issued the threat in a mumbling voice and with a physical frailty that was the delight of cartoonists. But few doubted he had the clout while alive to deliver the vote.
